figures.caption: Figure 3: Planned federated distributed intelligence architecture (not yet implemented). Each deployed ML Defender node operates fully autonomously; anonymized flow-level telemetry is contributed to a central aggregation tier for periodic retraining. Updated classifiers are packaged as Ed25519-signed plugins (ADR-025) and distributed to the fleet. All detection and response decisions remain local to each node; no live network metadata leaves the deployment site. This architecture is a post-pipeline-stabilization milestone; a future revision of this paper will document the implementation.

Figure 1: ML Defender end-to-end pipeline. Six components communicate over ZeroMQ with Protocol Buffers serialization and ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption. etcd-server distributes JSON configuration at startup. The dual-score Maximum Threat Wins policy (Eq. 1) selects the arithmetic maximum of Fast Detector and ML Detector scores; the RAG subsystem provides semantic observability over the live event stream.

Figure 2: Representative high-availability deployment of ML Defender in a hospital environment. A primary node monitors all inbound and inter-segment traffic via NIC 1 (monitored); a warmstandby node receives heartbeat signals and promotes automatically on primary failure. Both nodes run the full six-component pipeline on commodity hardware. etcd-server and the RAG query interface are co-located on the primary node. Firewall ACL Agent topology: scored Protocol Buffers events flow from ml-detector to one or more firewall-acl-agent instances, which apply ipset/iptables rules at the relevant boundary. A single gateway node requires one agent; each independent segment with its own firewall requires its own agent instance. etcd-server is shown in single-node mode (current implementation); a distributed HA etcd cluster is in the project backlog. Peer-to-peer seed negotiation is under design.
